title: Even students’ worst-case thesis deadlines turned out too optimistic
body: Kahneman and Tversky named the planning fallacy in 1979: we underestimate the time, costs and risks of what we plan to do. In a 1994 study, Buehler, Griffin and Ross asked students when they would finish their theses. The average estimate was 33.9 days; asked for the worst case, if everything went as badly as possible, they said 48.6 days. The actual average was **55.5 days**, and only about 30% finished by their predicted date. The bias applies only to our own tasks: outside observers tend to be pessimistic and overestimate how long a job will take.

slides.question: The students predicted 33.9 days on average. How long did finishing actually take?
slides.explanation: The actual average was 55.5 days, beyond even the students’ worst-case estimate of 48.6. Only about 30% finished on time.

slides.heading: Famous overruns
items: Sydney Opera House: expected 1963 for $7 million; a scaled-down version opened in 1973 for $102 million
Denver International Airport: opened sixteen months late
Eurofighter Typhoon: six years longer than expected
Boston’s Big Dig: finished seven years later than planned

slides.heading: The fix: look outside
slides.text: Why does it happen? People focus on the task ahead rather than on how similar tasks went before, and blame past delays on outside events. One remedy is reference class forecasting: predict the outcome from the actual outcomes of a whole class of similar projects, not from your plan.

slides.question: Whose time estimates tend to be too pessimistic rather than too optimistic?
slides.explanation: The planning fallacy affects predictions about our own tasks. When outsiders predict someone else’s task, they tend to overestimate the time needed.
